utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. You may be seated. Good morning to the technical booth, the interpreters, legal assistants, and court reporters; good morning, Madam Registrar; good morning, Ms. Hollis, Mr. Waidyaratne, Mr. Piacente; good morning, Defence counsel. They're all here, I see. Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we continue, can everyone follow? Can we hear each other well? Fine. You're going to continue to answer questions put to you today. It is the turn of the Defence counsel of Mr. Zigic. I remind you that you are still under oath. So Mr. Tosic and Mr. Stojanovic, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I have to use the pseudonym N in addressing you. Mr. Zigic's defence, composed of my colleague Mr. Tosic from Banja Luka and myself, Slobodan Stojanovic from Belgrade, has a few questions for you. During your testimony yesterday, you stated that you had known Mr. Zigic before Keraterm as a taxi driver from Prijedor. Can you tell us a little more about that, how you came to meet him? Did you use his services? Did you see him driving a taxi, or in some other way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt about him seeing him driving a taxi, and I saw him washing his car at Trisvic's, and I know that his relatives live near Kozarac. That's all I know about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where would you see Mr. Zigic as a taxi driver, what part of town or in the suburbs? Roughly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him twice at the Prijedor railway station.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what car he drove as a taxi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether it was a Fiat or a Lada.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the colour of the car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was beige, cream coloured.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in what period of time you saw him as a taxi driver? I'm not asking for any precision.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the years before the war, in 1991 and 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But in 1992 the war had already broken out. So you mean until the actual outbreak of the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You described his appearance before you saw him in Keraterm, and you said, among other things, that he had a scar on his face. Could you describe that scar in greater detail, what part of the face?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is on his chin somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question was: You noticed the scar before you met him in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You have already almost answered that question. Did you ever have personal contacts with Zigic before Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1994, I have noted the date of the 26th of September as the date when you gave a written statement to the Prosecution of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you state on that occasion that in the first seven days of your stay in Keraterm, as far as you knew, some 50 men had been released after having been interrogated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to the event with Emsud Bahonjic, and I have a few questions regarding that for you. Do you know the circumstances under which Emsud was arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Emsud was arrested in Kozarac near the taxi cafe bar, in the reserve police force, wearing that uniform. He had a rifle on him from which he had not shot a single bullet, and two or three others were arrested with him and were executed on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that he was a kind of fighter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not a combatant. He was a member of the reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But he had a rifle. Did he have ammunition too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the rifle was issued to him by the public security station of Prijedor, like all active duty and reserve policemen of Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Within which police organisation was he at the moment of arrest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a member of the Yugoslav reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, you said that he was brought on the 8th or 9th of June. So he had been arrested just prior to that. Did a Yugoslav police force exist at that time in that part of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that Emsud was brought on the 8th or 9th of June to the camp. So I assume he was arrested the day before, that very same day, but that is not important. And you said when he was arrested, he was a member of the Yugoslav police. My question is: At that point in time, that is, beginning of June, did a Yugoslav police force exist at all in that part of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Yugoslav police still existed then, and he was arrested two, three, or five days before his arrival in Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know perhaps a little more about the police unit he belonged to and who was in command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zigic, from the village of Balte was with him, but I don't know his first name. He was with him in the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You said he arrived in Keraterm on the 8th or 9th of June. Was he already beaten up? Do you know who beat him up previously?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Dusan Knezevic, called Duca.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the Prosecution, did you say that Emsud told you at the time, if Duca or Dusan Knezevic comes, I'm finished?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But Zoran Zigic came at the same time and nicknamed him the sniper from Singapore.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the reason why the late Emsud feared Duca so much?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In that same statement, did you say that Emsud was beaten for the following 19 or 20 days, on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you say in that statement that Emsud died in the afternoon? I think it was the 26th of June.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made that statement a long time ago, and I don't remember very well. I still haven't read that statement, and you have studied it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can I remind you? Can I refresh your memory then? It is page 13 of the Bosnian or Serbian version. It doesn't matter which. Second paragraph from the top, and it says: "Emsud died in the afternoon. I think it was the 26th of June." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In that same statement, did you say that Emsud was beaten by Dusan Knezevic, Zoran Zigic, Predrag Banovic, a concern Sahadija, and a certain Kondic? Of course, this was not simultaneously, but did all these persons participate in beating Emsud Bahonjic according to what you said in that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: They all participated but Zoran Zigic beat him the most, then Dusan Knezevic, and then young Predrag Banovic as third.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In that same statement, did you say that Duca participated about ten times in beating up Emsud?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whoever was called out from any room, Emsud was among them, because that was the order given by Zigic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But my question was: Did you say that Duca participated about ten times in beating up Emsud?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you also mention a very bad beating that Emsud received from Predrag Banovic when Emsud happened to be alone in the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recollect that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the Court's indulgence, I should like to read from page 17, the one but last paragraph: "Once when I was standing in line for food in front of the room in which I was held at the time, I saw that Emsud was the only one left in room number 2. I saw Predrag Banovic go to him. I heard Emsud screaming. When I went back towards Emsud, the whole left side of his face was completely deformed. When this happened, there was no one else there but Banovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see Zoran Zigic in Keraterm together with any one of the Banovic brothers that you mentioned, together?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, when, if it wasn't frequently?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was when the Banovics were on duty as guards, Zigic could come into the camp at his will.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in what period of time this occurred? More precisely, when were the Banovics on duty, on guard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well perhaps I wasn't quite clear enough. Were they there from the very beginning when you arrived in Keraterm, as guards in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three or four days later, they started coming to Keraterm as guards in Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After your arrival?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after my arrival in Keraterm. And they stayed until the end of my stay in Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: A few questions in connection with an individual known as Car. Can you tell us, in somewhat more detail, when the event -- when somebody was forced to run with a machine-gun, roughly when does this happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened in the afternoon. It was raining. I do not recollect the date because it was a long time ago, but it was in the second or third half of my stay in the camp. I mean in the -- no. In the second or third week of my stay in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us anything more as to when Car died?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in the night, but I saw his body the next day in front of the door of the toilet, about seven or eight metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us clarify a certain detail, if we may. You told us yesterday that he died the next day after this event, if I am not mistaken. And in this statement, on page 14, it says that you told the Prosecution that he died one hour after this incident. Is it correct that you said that then? So could you explain that in greater detail?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: He died an hour after that running, but I saw his body the next day, thrown out opposite the door of the toilet, at a distance of some seven or eight metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Regarding Sengin Ramadanovic, in your statement to the Prosecution, did you say that he was beaten by Zigic, Banovic, and Duca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When did you see Zigic for the last time in Keraterm? I think you told us you were there from the 31st of May until you went to Trnopolje on the 6th of August, 1992. Can you tell us when you saw him for the last time? If you don't know the date, then tell us in relation to a certain event.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him for the last time in the Trnopolje camp, when we arrived from Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That is in Trnopolje. But my question is when you saw him for the last time in Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you link that somehow to your period of stay? So far you have been talking about the first, second, and third week of your stay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You told us a little about the event or, rather, the massacre in room number 3. If I understood you correctly, you were taken out in the morning to pile up the bodies, as you said, between rooms number 3 and 4. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After that, did you say that shortly after that, a truck arrived for the bodies to be loaded on it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the truck arrived later for the bodies to be loaded onto it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Zigic close to that truck, close to that truck, right next to the truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him that day in the camp, but I can't say that I saw him next to the truck. I really can't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us where you saw him that day in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether he was near the scales or not, I'm not quite sure, but I know that I saw him moving around in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You said "on that day." What time of day was it? Was it in the morning, midday, the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that all the bodies had already been collected and had started to be loaded onto the truck, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The machine-gun or machine-guns, were they positioned in front of the rooms in which the people were detained in Keraterm, even before this night when the tragedy occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: The machine-gun nest was just behind the scales and just in front of the scales.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. The question was: Did it exist before too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But that night a truck arrived which was never there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, since when was the machine-gun nest positioned there? Was it from the very first time you arrived or was it formed later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they put the wire at number 1 and number 2, they positioned the machine-gun nest, but I can't remember the date. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and english transcripts

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You don't have to give us the date, but just tell us which week.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the third or fourth week of my stay in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that a machine-gun nest existed several days prior to this massacre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The machine-gun nest existed at two places, but that night a truck came from which most of the shooting came and from which most of the fire could be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The massacre, did you describe it in detail to the investigators of the Prosecution in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In that statement, did you describe a large number of incidents with Zigic, other incidents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In that same statement, in describing this tragedy, did you mention Zigic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me put a direct question to you. On the day of the gunfire and this dreadful massacre, did you see Zigic then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think the night before the massacre was the 24th. Of course you may not remember the exact date, but the evening prior to the shooting of men in room number 3, did you see Zoran Zigic somewhere in the vicinity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember whether I did or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your indulgence, I should like to ask a few questions relative to some protected witnesses. So I think it would be advisable to provide them with maximum protection and, therefore, go into a private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are already in public session. Mr. Waidyaratne, do you have any additional questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Waidyaratne. Judge Riad has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Witness N, good morning. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I have just two questions perhaps to ask you for more clarification, or for more information. You were once called by the guard called Kajin to pile bodies between room 3 and 4. Bodies were being pulled out from rooms 3 and 4 and you described the bodies as some of them had no backs and some had no arms. Were these people without arms and backs alive or dead? Were all the people inside the room being pulled out dead?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all dead. They were all dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So nobody survived from inside the rooms? They died inside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This only took place in room number 3, and some people survived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What took place when you say this took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole activity, the shooting incident occurred in room number 3 and in front of room number 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Shooting inside, inside the room itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shooting was going on on that night in front of the room and inside the room itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And the people who lost their backs and their arms, the shooting does not -- was it shooting by bullets or by cannons to lose the back or to lose the arms? To your knowledge, what happened? Was it bombs, was it what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shooting was from a large calibre machine-gun from which fire was opened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, you also were called, I think, to load the corpses on the truck which came. Now, all the people which were loaded -- you said to load corpses and wounded -- were they put together in the same truck, one over the other, or were the wounded treated differently from the dead?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was ordered to collect them and put them on a pile, and others were ordered to load them onto the truck, and the wounded also were loading the dead onto the truck, and at the end the wounded also boarded the truck together with the bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mean they were piled together, dead and wounded? How were the wounded treated, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: The wounded were ordered to board the truck which was carrying dead bodies, and they were all taken away on the same truck, and no medical assistance was ever given to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Riad. Madam Judge Wald has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Two brief questions, Witness N. You mentioned that when the Banovics were on duty as guards, that Zigic could come into the camp at will, and you saw him several times with one of the Banovics. Was that the only time that Zigic, to your knowledge, could come into the camp at will when these people, the Banovics, were on duty or was he there at other times as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would come whenever he wanted to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So is wasn't just certain guards that could decide whether he would come or not. He came whenever he wished, regardless of who was on duty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. My second question is just to make sure that I understood your answer to one of the questions asked by Mr. Zigic's counsel, and that is: Around the time of the alleged massacre, am I correct that you didn't see Zigic around the gun placement the afternoon before the shootings, and you didn't see him around the truck the morning after the shootings when you were piling bodies? I just want to make sure I have that correct. Is that right? Or you don't remember whether you saw them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't load the bodies at all. I just pulled them out. And Zigic was walking around the scales which was located in front of the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. That's what I wanted to get straight. I understand you now to be saying that when you were doing the piling of the bodies, Zigic was walking around somewhere in the vicinity, around the scales that were located in front; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald. Witness N, I have a question. Actually, I need some clarification. You stated that you would see Zigic in the camp every day, and you linked the presence of Zigic with the presence of another guard at one point. Could you tell us the frequency of your sightings of Zigic in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the frequency, I can say that I saw him every day. Sometimes he would come and stay only for one hour, sometimes 20 minutes. On another occasion for two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you perhaps know whether Zigic had any functions over there? Did he have any specific duties as part of the security personnel? You were able to observe the situation on a daily basis, so did you reach any conclusion in that respect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he had no function whatsoever, because he would come -- because there were shifts in the camp, and I didn't see him in any of those shifts. He would come whenever he wished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, he did not have any particular schedule?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS N [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness N. I don't think we have any other questions for you except perhaps to ask you whether you have anything to say, anything that has not been asked of you here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that we have any documents that need to be tendered into evidence, Mr. Waidyaratne?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards the Defence of Mr. Zigic, no exhibits? Thank you. Witness N, thank you very much for coming to testify here. We wish you a pleasant journey back to your place of residence. Please do not move for a second because the blinds need to be lowered down and only after that can you be taken out of the courtroom by the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis, what happens next?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness will be Witness AM. This witness will be testifying with a pseudonym and with image distortion but not with voice distortion, and Mr. Piacente will be leading the direct evidence of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The registrar has told me that we need a short break to make all the necessary preparations, because it seems that we no longer need the voice distortion. So certain technical changes have to be made. So we will have a very brief break, only a five-minute break to make the necessary arrangements. --- Break taken at 10.15 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness AM, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will be referred to as Witness AM because of the protective measures. Could you please read the solemn declaration that the usher is giving you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may now be seated. Make yourself comfortable. Are you comfortable, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness AM, you are first going to answer questions put to you by the Prosecutor, who is represented here by Mr. Piacente. Mr. Piacente, you have the floor. Oh, I'm sorry. There is some something that we have to do before. Witness, could you please have a look at the piece of paper that the usher will show you, and could you tell us by simply saying yes or no whether this is indeed your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Now the examination can proceed. Mr. Piacente, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PIACENTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Before I start, Your Honour, I would like to specify that Witness AM is being called to testify about his personal data; his arrest; his confinement in Trnopolje and Omarska; the ethnicity of prisoners; ethnicity of soldiers; treatment suffered by him and other prisoners in Omarska; killings the night between 11th and 12th of July, 1992, St. Peter's Day; killings of detainees from Hambarine; impact on the victim of the crimes committed by the accused. Another request: May we go into private session for a while, just for a few questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Piacente, we are in public session again.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you stay in Trnopolje in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And then where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: According to some special lists or indictments, they were looking for drivers who had been charged with arms smuggling from Croatia into Bosnia, and I was amongst those people and I was taken to Omarska to be interrogated there.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And were you interrogated in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: I was interrogated on the same day I arrived in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Who were you interrogated by?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: I was interrogated by two individuals in uniform whom I didn't know. Later, according to some information that we had, we knew that people from Banja Luka would come for interrogations in Omarska. There was a policeman there who would hit the person who was being interrogated if the investigators were not pleased with the answers.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So you were interrogated, two policemen interrogated you. Who else was present during your interrogation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: There was one civilian who was standing behind my back and who was also present during my interrogation.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What were you asked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: The first question was posed almost while I was at the door. They asked me how many guns I had smuggled for Muslims in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was it only that question or were you asked other questions? If you can list them, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: There were other questions as well, such as who had organised the defence in Kozarac, who had armed people, who had paid the people for that, what my role in those activities was, whom I had voted for, why we didn't want to live in Yugoslavia. So they wanted to know everything about this prewar situation.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Yes, I was. During the interrogation, I sustained numerous blows with clubs. I didn't fall down, I didn't faint, but I was black and blue all over my back.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Who were you beaten by? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and english transcripts

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: I was beaten by a civilian who was standing in the corner of the room behind my back.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Where were you confined in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: When the interrogation ended, we could eat. We had dinner, and then we were transferred to an electrical workshop in the building above the garages where the machines were repaired. There was an electrical workshop, and that is where I was detained.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Which floor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: The first floor.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did other people arrive the first night of your confinement in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: While we waited in line for dinner, a group of people arrived who had been captured at Benkovac, two buses full, and who were getting off the bus just then and being confined in the room behind the kitchen, some sort of garages. Those men were running from the buses, and they had to pass between two lines of Serb guards who hit them as they ran towards this garage. The group numbered about 150 or 120 men. We didn't count them, but there were two buses full.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Were you registered when you arrived in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Yes. When we were interrogated, they asked me about my personal particulars, where I was born, my ID card. The documents I had on me I had to show them.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were also the other prisoners registered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: When people were interrogated, everyone had to say his name. And later on, as we stayed in the camp, lists were made. We were all forced out of rooms, and when we went back in, everyone had to pass by a table, give his name, and confirm this with a document or with witnesses who could confirm their identity if they had no documents on them.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: During your confinement in Omarska, did you have to give money to the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Money was a great attraction for all the guards, the leadership of the camp and generally. Money was always requested. So as not to kill somebody, we would have to collect so much money. Then half an hour later they would come back with the same request. At first there was some money, but very soon, a week or two later, the money had been taken from the people and then a collection of money was organised among people who were assumed to have hidden some money at home, because everyone knew that no one kept their money in the bank in Yugoslavia in those days because of inflation. People kept foreign currency which they needed for their business, at home.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: How much money did you give?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: I had to make a drawing, a diagram, and two men took it and they said they hadn't found my money at home. I had about 15.000 German marks.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Let's focus now on St. Peter's Day. Can you remember what happened that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: On the eve of St. Peter's Day, it is customary among the Serb people to light bonfires, to rejoice, to drink, and we would see that in the past, and the same happened that year. In that bonfire, they set fire to a large tyre of at least two metres in diameter, and as they orgied, they threw individuals into that fire. All this was happening in front of the "white house."

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: When you say "individuals," do you mean prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: When I say "individuals," they are prisoners, Muslims who were thrown into the fire by the guards who were standing around.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: How long did this ceremony last?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: The ceremony went on for several hours. I was at the window watching, and everybody wanted to look. We were pushing one another around to watch. This went on for a couple of hours, but I was at the window for a very short time, and I saw a young man being thrown in. And an acquaintance of mine, who was his neighbour, who was standing next to me, said his name was Cirkic, he was Captain Cirkic's brother who apparently had organised the defence of Kozarac, and he had been thrown into this burning tyre.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Among the prisoners, do you recall people from Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: The people from Hambarine, one afternoon in the second half of July, were brought there in two buses and put up in premises that we called the hangar or the rooms number 15 and number 26. Then a couple of hours later, those same people were all told to get out and all of them were put up in the "white house." This was just before darkness fell.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was the "white house" one of the premises of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Yes. The "white house" was across the way from this main building. I can show it. I slept in an office upstairs in this building occasionally, and I had a direct view of the "white house" from there, and I could see what was happening to people who were taken that night to the "white house."

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And can you tell us what happened that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: That night I fell asleep very late, as usual, about 10.00 or 11.00, and roughly at 2.00 or 3.00 a.m. I was awakened by pistol shots behind the building. I got up cautiously, I passed by a lemon plant that was in a pot, and I saw people lying on the ground, lots of people, and guards would go by and fire a bullet in their heads to finish them off. I didn't see how they fell to the ground and how they were tortured. Probably they were beaten by various things, fire extinguishers, clubs, poles, and then the killing took place with pistol shots, one bullet each into the head. I remember well when this bullet was fired, the brain would come out as if the bullet had hit milk, and it came out like white dust.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the guards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Only one guard I could recognise, his name was Zivko Marmat, because he had unusually fair hair, the only one among all the guards who came to the camp. He was the fairest. He was blonde.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Where had the victims been confined before their arrival in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: According to what the people who survived the massacre said, but they didn't want to report, they were held in Keraterm for a month or two.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: How do you know it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: This was established after we arrived at Manjaca and when we all got together so we could contact one another. And a man surnamed Tadic, I don't know his first name, said that he stayed behind and his whole group of neighbours and acquaintance, who were apparently sent for exchange, actually went to the "white house." Then I told him they never went to be exchanged, they were all killed that night.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you specify where were the bodies of the victims were lying when they were shot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: The bodies of the victims lay around the "white house," behind the "white house," on the side towards the "red house," on the concrete, on the asphalt pista behind the "red house." Simply, I was horrified when I saw so many bodies lying there, some 50 or 70 metres, in an area of some 50 or 70 metres.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What happened to the corpses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: After these bullets were fired into people's heads, a truck came and a loader, and then they took out two detainees, two prisoners from behind the wire, and they had to load these bodies into the scoop of the loader for the loader to load them onto the truck. Four or five of these scoopfuls had to be loaded onto one truck. Then those bodies would be driven away somewhere, and then the truck would return 10 or 15 minutes later, and this happened five or six times.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you describe this truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: The truck was a FAP truck, F-A-P, it was a 19/21 model. It was a loader. It's capacity was seven to eight cubic metres of loading space.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Where was the office, where you were sleeping in that night, located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: The office was on the first floor of this building here. I don't know how deep inside it was, but it was roughly opposite the "white house."

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What was the distance between you and the corpses, the whole scene? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: The closest bodies were at a distance of 20 metres perhaps, and those furthest away were behind the "red house," as far as I could see. I couldn't see well, but I could see a little thanks to the lamps that were lighted next to the "white house." So the greatest distance was 70 metres between me and the bodies furthest away from me.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: How many times a day were you used to being fed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: As a rule, we ate once a day. However, if we were moved and if the timetable was changed and if we were last in order, the last two or three groups in order would get nothing that day, so that over a period of two weeks, there was a great possibility of going without any food for one day during that two-week period.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Were you beaten during your meals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Yes. During meals, people had to run, and entering the canteen there was a bend, and they would pour water on the ground. People would slip and fall. They would be beaten and then go and eat like that. And coming back from the canteen, they had to make this bend again, and again they would fall and again they would be beaten. There would be groups of 30 going to the canteen to eat. Everything had to be done very quickly. When they said, "That's it," we will to leave regardless of whether you had finished your meal or not.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: I stayed in Omarska a little under two and a half months.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And then where were you confined?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Then a fatal transport occurred. A selection of people in Omarska, of people who were sent to Trnopolje, another group to Manjaca, and a last group remained as a showcase for the public, to show them that this was a small centre, that it was no concentration camp, that it was an investigation centre. Then two days later, after representatives of the International Community visited them, the doctors without frontiers who got a good impression of people being fed regularly, being free to move, being able to wash and bathe, then a large group was transferred to Manjaca and an equally large group to Trnopolje. We travelled for a long time to Manjaca. We left just before nightfall, and I don't remember exactly for how long, late into the night. During the trip the buses were stopped, and individuals were asked to get off. Why and by whom I don't know. There were little lists going around and notes, but nothing unusual happened before we reached Manjaca. We all spent that night in buses. The camp commander would not let men get off the buses at night, so we had to spend the night in the buses. In the morning, we were all forced off the buses. Then again lists were being made. People could already have been recognised. We all had to squat to be searched, and then a certain number of people from that group were separated to one side and killed some 50 metres away from us. They were later loaded onto a bus and thrown next to the Vrbas River at Banja Luka. We heard this later from people who had relatives in Banja Luka, that those bodies were found and that they were buried.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PIACENTE
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the help of the usher, can Witness AM be shown Exhibit 377D? It is a diagram.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Witness AM, looking at this diagram, can you please point to the room, the place from which you saw the guards shooting the prisoners from Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Could you please turn the picture around by 180 degrees? I'm not sure whether it was this office or this one.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you tell us the numbers? Yes, there are some letters and numbers on the place that you pointed. Can you tell us which numbers are they? Which numbers did you point to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: It says B19 here and B18, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Okay. Can you please point to the room where you were usually confined, the electricity workshop?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PIACENTE
utterances.text: Can Witness AM be shown Exhibit 382.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me for interrupting you, but for the record, we have to say that it is Exhibit 3/77 to make sure that things are quite correct. It's not 377 but 3/77. Otherwise, we will run into problems. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PIACENTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. As well, I think that the exhibit that is now being shown to Witness AM is 3/82. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PIACENTE
utterances.text: This is the exhibit I was looking for. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Witness AM, can you point to the room from which you said that you saw the guards shooting the prisoners from Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Roughly here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PIACENTE
utterances.text: Is it possible for the witness to mark with a pen the place that he has identified? Okay. I withdraw the question. Thanks. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you identify, can you point, please, to the place where you saw the bodies lying down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: The bodies were lying around the "white house," in this area, and behind the "red house."

utterances.speaker: MR. PIACENTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No more questions for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PIACENTE
utterances.text: No more questions for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now is the time for the cross-examination, but I see it is almost 11.00. So perhaps we should have a break now and then resume for the cross-examination. In that way, the Defence will have sufficient time to prepare. Witness, please don't move for the moment. The usher is going to pull down the blinds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we're going to have a half-hour break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Mr. Simic, what is going to be the order of the cross-examination, please? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Fila and myself will be the only ones to cross-examine the witness; first Mr. Fila and then myself. The rest of the Defence team have no questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Simic. Witness AM, you're now going to answer questions that will be put to you by Mr. Krstan Simic. Mr. Simic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness AM.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: I have only a few questions for you concerning your testimony here and also concerning the statement that you gave to the representatives of the Tribunal. You said that you had spent a period of time in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How long were you there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Two or three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Were you arrested or did you come to Trnopolje on your own?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: On the third day of the shelling of Kozarac, a military vehicle Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and english transcripts came to my house and we were told to gather, all of us, from the Sora street, and we were ordered to move towards Prijedor where we were supposed to stay for a few days until the situation calms down. So we set out for Prijedor but not alone the main Banja Luka road but via the Suhi Brod village and then across the Prijedor-Banja Luka road junction in the direction of the village of Orlovci. And before we reached the village of Orlovci, we were taken to a side road, a dirt road, which led to Trnopolje. We passed by a school, a local community centre, and this is where we spent two or three nights. We were still on buses or trucks, and this is how we reached Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: If I have understood you correctly, you were ordered to march, to walk towards that location.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Initially, the idea was for us to walk. However, there was a misunderstanding. We finally went to Trnopolje by buses, by trucks, and other vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You stated that you had gone to Omarska after Trnopolje. On what day did you reach Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: On Tuesday evening, we arrived in the Trnopolje camp, and then two days later, on Friday afternoon, I was taken to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Could you tell us the date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: The date. I'm not sure what date it was. I know it was a Friday. I could perhaps take a look at the calendar.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What month was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: It was in late May or the beginning of June. I cannot tell you the exact date. It is either the 31st of May or the 1st of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You told us that you had been put up in a warehouse, electrical appliances warehouse, and that your room was on the first floor.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you stay in that room throughout your stay in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Until the 12th or the 13th of July, I slept in that room all the time. After that, the door of the office was broken into, so during the night I would go to that office and spend the night there. The room was on the same floor in the same corridor, at the end of the corridor; that's where the office was. I would never stay there during the day, only during the night. Throughout my stay there, I was on the same floor and the same corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: The room in which you were at that time, did it have any windows, and if so, how many and how big were they, if you can tell us that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: You mean the big warehouse or the office?

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: The room where you spent your days.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: The room had very large windows looking on one side, and the windows went along the wall, covering the whole length of the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What about the glass on those windows of that room, was it transparent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Yes, it was. There was a railing which was perhaps one metre and one metre 20 centimetres high, and there was a glass pane above. I don't know whether there was another railing above that one, but the windows were rather large.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: So you're telling me that there was one railing. You're not sure about the other one. Try to remember the room, and if you can, could you please tell us how high was that closed area without glass?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: If I compare it to a human being, it was a little above the waist.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where did the windows look onto?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: The windows were facing the meadow, between the "red house" and the "white house."

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: So you were able to see both houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Yes, if I looked to the left, I could see the "red house." If I looked to the right-hand side, I could see the "white house."

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You stated that after the 12th of July, you moved to another room which had been broken into. Could you tell us about the windows in that room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: It was the same kind of windows. They were rather large and also had a railing, a window sill.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What about the view from those windows?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: I was somewhat closer to the "white house" in that room. From that other room I couldn't see the "white house" directly, only if I looked towards the right-hand side could I see the "white house."

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Let me go back to the room where you spent your time up to the 12th of July. From that room, were you perhaps able to see the entrance door to the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I could see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Witness AM, during your stay in the first room, during the day, how much time would you spend outside these rooms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Well, I would go out for lunch and when I went to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where was the toilet located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: At the beginning, we had two toilets on the same floor, but they were closed down after awhile and were not being used. Later on, we were using the toilet which was on the ground floor of the big hall near a staircase which led outside from that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, the toilet was inside the large hangar building.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Yes, it was inside this building.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned your interrogation. You also told us the circumstances about that interrogation. My question in relation to that is the following: Was the individual who was beating you during the interrogation under the authority of the investigators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You also testified that other individuals had been interrogated as well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Yes, in the adjacent room.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Witness AM, do you have any knowledge, any information whether during those days or after your interrogation, whether there were any releases of detainees who had been interrogated, and if so, what was it all about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: People were interrogated in great numbers in groups on a daily basis, and at the end of the day, a group of people would be called out which would subsequently be transferred to Trnopolje. This went on for the first ten days, and after that, even that stopped and not a single person was released before the closing down of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: So some people were transferred from Omarska to Trnopolje after the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: I should like to discuss your statement, the statement that you gave to the investigators of the Tribunal. Did you talk to the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Some time ago, quite awhile ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What do you mean by that, "awhile ago."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Well, in 1994. Yes, I gave a statement in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: On that occasion, did you talk to Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: I don't remember the names of those people at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you give that statement on your own?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: On your own free will?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you talk about everything you could remember at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Yes. My recollection was much better in those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Yes. Let us discuss the period of time before your arrival in Trnopolje. You spoke at some length in that statement about the events in Kozarac, about the arming of the population and similar events. Were there any military or paramilitary organisations in Kozarac prior to the attack on Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: There were two men who were in Kozarac who were detained, who had been in detention and were criminals, and declared themselves as soldiers, and they bought some weapons from Serbs. They organised two or three small groups of people, according to the ideas that they had at the time. They played war games and certain things happened after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Witness AM, did they have any uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Well, they had uniforms that they had bought from the army. Those were camouflage uniforms. Sometimes they would wear them and go out. Sometimes they wore civilian clothes. They did that as they pleased. They acted on their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you remember their names or nicknames?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I remember Kole, Ramiz Cirkin, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you know the person by the name of Sead Cirkin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: I didn't know Sead Cirkin personally. He was an officer of the former JNA. He had come to Kozarac sometime prior to the war, and he put every single male name on the list of members of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, an army without tanks or rockets or soldiers is just a dead letter on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: In your statement, you mentioned the weapons that belonged to the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Could you remember the number, the quantity of those weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: The weapons consisted mainly of very old Tandzara rifles, M-48 rifles, that's what they called them. And the rest of the weapons had been withdrawn a few months prior to that to the barracks in Banja Luka. The Territorial Defence had very few rifles left and most of them were very old rifles, 50 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Witness AM, you have stated that your recollection was much better in those days, which is perfectly understandable. Let me quote from page 11 of your statement. "The Territorial Defence has distributed a number of weapons. Part of those weapons had been illegally bought from Serbs. A number of people had simply carried those weapons with them in the woods where they were hiding themselves. Some of that weaponry was taken to Croatia, and it is believed that the army of the Territorial Defence had about 400 automatic rifles and a few pieces of hand-held rocket launchers. One individual from the army had to register the number of weapons possessed by everyone. It was one of my neighbours and a commander of one of the groups that I have mentioned before. He learnt that the Territorial Defence had about 400 pieces of weapons."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: I don't think I've ever said anything about hand-held rocket launchers, and I don't think that I said that the weapons had gone to Croatia. As regards the number, yes, that is familiar to me, 400 pieces of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: In your statement, you also spoke about a great number of people who had bought weapons. Was that the case? Was there any illegal traffic of weapons at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you buy a rifle for yourself, in view of the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What kind of rifle was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: It was an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you ever request a permit for that rifle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Do you know of any other similar cases, other people from your community who acted the same way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Well, if you have a number of 400 rifles, then you probably had 400 rifle owners, but I didn't know them personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Witness AM, let me go back to Kole's and Ramiz's groups, as you call them. When did they come into existence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Well, could you perhaps situate it in time in respect of the attack on Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Well, then a couple of months before the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, you stated that those groups had killed some Serbs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: I don't know whether that is correct. I was never present at any such incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Let me go back once again to the beginning, and this will be the end of my cross-examination. As regards the ethnic composition of the people who were members of those two paramilitary or military formations and the formation which was created by Sead Cirkin, what was the ethnic composition of those people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Most of them were Muslims. There were several Croats there perhaps. The Galiani people were also there but they were sitting on the fence for a while. They didn't know which way to go. Finally they sided Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and english transcripts with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: As regards your transfer from Trnopolje to Omarska, how did that occur?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Two individuals in uniform arrived in a car with the list of people they were looking for. Five people were being looked for. They found three people and three of us were taken to Omarska. This is how we were transferred to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How were you taken there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: We were taken in a red Jugo 45 vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You mentioned two individuals in uniform. Judging from their uniforms, which group did they belong to? Were they members of the police, of the army, or some other group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. They were not active duty soldiers or active duty policemen, so I really wouldn't know which army they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Does it mean that they were not members of the active police force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: No, they were not active duty policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: During the transport from Trnopolje to Omarska, were you mistreated in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: No. We were only threatened while we were in Kozarusa. A man who was at the checkpoint was looking for us. He wanted us to be taken out of the car. He wanted to slaughter us, and he said that we didn't need any interrogation, but that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: That is, you were not mistreated or tied by your escort?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: No, we were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness AM. This concludes my cross-examination. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Simic. Mr. Toma Fila has the floor now. Your witness, Mr. Toma Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I shall be brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Good morning to you. My name is Mr. Toma Fila. I'm an attorney from Belgrade, and together with my colleague, Jovanovic, I'm defence counsel for Mladjo Radic. If I understood you correctly, you described the events on the eve of St. Peter's Day, and you were looking from the first room.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: I can show you on the model.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It is the room you showed the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: The office, no. Not from the office. I watched this event from the office with the people from Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But the event on St. Peter's Day from another room. So you were transferred there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: No. I could move freely between the office and that room along the corridor of 20 metres or so. The distance was some 20 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You've confused me I'm afraid. Is it the room you find yourself in after being transferred on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: From the 12th of July or, rather, two or three days later, I would occasionally sleep in the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And was it then when the event occurred with the fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: It was on the 11th of July in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So on today's day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Yes, to be quite precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, the interpreters are asking you to make pauses, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where was the fire burning in relation to the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: In front of the "white house." Maybe a metre or two away. It wasn't in front of the entrance. To one side.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said you recognised only one person called Marmat.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: No. On that occasion I didn't recognise anyone. We're not talking about the same incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Then my question is why you didn't recognise anyone. In other words --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: I didn't know these people. I have never known them, with the exception of this Marmat. It was quite dark, and I didn't know those people. I could recognise Marmat because he had this exceptionally fair hair and he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So the reason that you didn't recognise them was the fact that you didn't know them and not poor visibility.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Well, visibility contributed to it, but you could see what men were doing. You couldn't read any letters on them, but you could see what an individual was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you give a statement to the Prosecutor on the 26th of August and the 30th of August, 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let me read you a passage: "Zivko Marmat was there throughout, but I don't know whether he was next to the fire."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: So?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I see. So you abide by this statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So the fire was lit that evening. What happened the next morning when the fire stopped burning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you see any body there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: There was this pile left, the black ashes from the tyre, but what was there, nobody went to look.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This Cirkin, is his name Siad or Sead, or are there two people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: The man who knew him and who watched the event with me said he was the brother of Captain Cirkic who wanted to organise the defence in Kozarac. What his first name is, I really don't know. It was his brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you were watching this fire of the truck tire, did anyone else see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Yes. This man who told me the name of this man.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What name is his? What is his name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Muhamed Cirkic, known as Krimi.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You spoke about food.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That you had to eat it up quickly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You also said two groups wouldn't have time to eat.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Two groups that were the last in order, the order was changed every day, and sometimes I was never the first to leave the room. I tried to be the last so as not to wait long in queue, so there were times when I, myself, got nothing to eat that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But why didn't you have time to get your food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: The food ran out. They ran out of food. That was the answer we were given.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was the reason why you had to eat quickly to give you all a chance to eat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: I don't know what the reason was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You told us that your memory was fresher when you gave that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why in the statement then did you not mention that when you were going to eat and coming back from your meals that you were beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: That statement, if I were to tell the whole story, would go on indefinitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: "We went in groups of 30 because that is the number of plates and cups they had." That's what you said in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Is that important?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The Judges will judge whether it is important, not us. You said you went in groups of 30 and that you couldn't see anyone.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: While we were waiting, we had to face the wall on the other side of this building. We had to face the wall. And while we were eating, you had to eat quickly and have your head bent down and not look around.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You spoke about this other event involving the people from Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You watched that incident from the office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: From the office, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was the visibility like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: It was summertime.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What time of day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: It was a nice clear night, a summer night. In the summer it's never totally dark, and there was a light in front of the "white house," so you could see quite well. You couldn't recognise a face, but you could see a group of people lying down, the shots being fired at those people. This was readily visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So you couldn't recognise a face?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: No, not of the guards, with the exception of this Marmat who had this exceptionally light-coloured hair, and he was the only one that I could identify by his hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was there a light in front of the "red house" perhaps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: What side do you mean? From the way I was looking at it, in front? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Whichever side, there are four sides to a house. Was there a light on any of those sides?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What part of the "red house" and the "white house" was in your plane of vision?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: I had the front facade of the "white house" and the backside of the "red house."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you explain then how you managed to see the bodies on all four sides of the white house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: If you're looking through the window, you can see over the "white house" bodies lying on the asphalt pista, and around the "white house" I could see around the three sides. Most of the bodies lay between the "white house" and the "red house" on the grass there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My last question: Were you personally beaten during your stay there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Only during my interrogation, and a couple of times I got a blow as we ran for food. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Piacente, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PIACENTE
utterances.text: No thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Witness AM, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I have a few questions, perhaps to see things more clearly. You mentioned at the beginning of your testimony, that you had to pay money in order not to be killed, I mean the detainees. Anybody could have been killed if they didn't pay money, or were some people on the list to be killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Some people were killed because of money, and there were lists that were compiled on the basis of other criteria from which people would be taken out, and from then on they would go missing to the present day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So to your knowledge, some people were just killed because they did not pay money?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: That, among other things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, you said that you had 15.000 Deutschemarks at home, and you drew a diagram and they went, and they said they didn't find it. What happened to you when they didn't find it, or was it just a pretext and they did find it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: Nothing happened to me after that. I was told, "Apparently your family has taken away your money." It's a shame they didn't find it, they said, because they would have given me some to buy something to eat, though I personally think that the money was found, because after that, they never bothered me nor looked for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, with regard to St. Peter's Day and the bonfire where they threw the large tyre. You saw, in fact, people thrown inside. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and english transcripts You mentioned even Captain Cirkic's brother. Were you close enough to see who it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
utterances.text: The fire was a big one, and one could clearly see a man being pushed into the fire. What the distance was, I couldn't say. You couldn't see the face of the man, you could just see the silhouette of the man. You could hear the screams very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was it only one man, or was it several people thrown in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AM
